title: A linked list is given where each node has a next pointer and an additional random pointer that can point to any node in the list or to null. Construct a deep copy of the list such that the copied nodes mirror the next and random structure without referencing any original node.
shortTitle: Copy List With Random Pointer — Interleave Clones or HashMap

s1_definition.profdef: Deep-copying a linked list with random pointers means creating brand-new nodes whose next and random pointers reproduce the original topology but point only into the copy. Two standard approaches exist: a HashMap from original node to clone node giving O(n) time and O(n) space, or the interleaving trick that weaves clones between originals to resolve random pointers in O(n) time and O(1) extra space.
s1_definition.analogy: The bank has a web of linked account records where each record points to the next record and also has a cross-reference arrow to some other arbitrary record, like a guarantor. The bank wants a completely separate photocopy of this whole web, where every arrow in the copy points to a copied record, never to an original. One way is to keep a lookup sheet mapping each original to its photocopy; a cleverer way is to slot each photocopy right behind its original temporarily so the cross-reference arrows are easy to redraw.
s1_definition.oneliner: Clone each node, then fix the random pointers using either a map from original to clone or by interleaving clones behind originals.
s1_definition.raw:
**Professional definition:** Deep-copying a linked list with random pointers means creating brand-new nodes whose next and random pointers reproduce the original topology but point only into the copy. Two standard approaches exist: a HashMap from original node to clone node giving O(n) time and O(n) space, or the interleaving trick that weaves clones between originals to resolve random pointers in O(n) time and O(1) extra space.

**In simple words (banking analogy):** The bank has a web of linked account records where each record points to the next record and also has a cross-reference arrow to some other arbitrary record, like a guarantor. The bank wants a completely separate photocopy of this whole web, where every arrow in the copy points to a copied record, never to an original. One way is to keep a lookup sheet mapping each original to its photocopy; a cleverer way is to slot each photocopy right behind its original temporarily so the cross-reference arrows are easy to redraw.

**One line to remember:** Clone each node, then fix the random pointers using either a map from original to clone or by interleaving clones behind originals.

sections.s2_technical:
The difficulty is the random pointer. The next pointers alone are easy to copy in one pass, but a random pointer may point forward or backward to a node we have not cloned yet, so we need a way to know, for any original node, what its clone is.

The HashMap approach is the most readable. In a first pass we create a clone of every node and store it: `Map<Node, Node> map = new HashMap<>(); for (Node cur = head; cur != null; cur = cur.next) map.put(cur, new Node(cur.val));`. In a second pass we wire up both pointers using the map: `for (Node cur = head; cur != null; cur = cur.next) { map.get(cur).next = map.get(cur.next); map.get(cur).random = map.get(cur.random); }`. Looking up `map.get(null)` returns null, which conveniently handles end-of-list and null random pointers. The copied head is `map.get(head)`.

The interleaving approach removes the map to achieve O(1) extra space. First we insert each clone right after its original: original A, clone A, original B, clone B. Then random pointers are trivial: for each original, `original.next.random = (original.random != null) ? original.random.next : null`, because an original's clone is always original.next and the random target's clone is always randomTarget.next. Finally we unweave the two lists to separate the copy from the original and restore the original.

A senior-level nuance is restoring the original list in the interleaving approach. Since we temporarily mutate the original by inserting clones, we must carefully split the interleaved list back into two clean lists, or we corrupt the caller's data.

Another nuance is choosing between the two: the HashMap version is simpler and I prefer it unless memory is genuinely constrained, because the interleaving version's pointer surgery is error-prone under time pressure.
sections.s3_banking:
Problem 1 — National Bank of India maintains a linked chain of loan guarantee records. Each record links to the next record in the chain and also has a guarantor pointer to some arbitrary other record in the same chain. For regulatory archiving, the bank must produce a fully independent deep copy of the entire chain so the archive can be frozen while the live chain keeps changing. This is exactly the copy-list-with-random-pointer problem, where the guarantor pointer is the random pointer.

Problem 2 — The copy must be truly independent: every next and guarantor pointer in the archive must point into the archive, never into the live chain, otherwise a later edit to the live chain would silently alter the frozen archive. This is what deep copy guarantees.

Problem 3 — Guarantor pointers can point forward or backward in the chain, so we cannot resolve them in a single naive pass; we use a HashMap from original record to its clone.

In the code: a `GuaranteeNode` holds a record id, a next pointer, and a guarantor pointer. A `ChainCopier` has a `deepCopy` method using the HashMap approach. A `CopyDemo` main builds a small guarantee chain with cross-references and prints the independent copy.

sections.s5_journey:
Input: chain G1, G2, G3 with next links G1 to G2 to G3, and guarantor links G1 to G3, G2 to G1, G3 to null.

Step 1 (first pass): We create clone-G1, clone-G2, clone-G3 and store each in the map keyed by its original. At this point the clones exist but have no pointers wired.

Step 2 (second pass, original G1): clone-G1.next becomes map.get(G2) which is clone-G2. clone-G1.guarantor becomes map.get(G3) which is clone-G3.

Step 3 (original G2): clone-G2.next becomes clone-G3. clone-G2.guarantor becomes map.get(G1) which is clone-G1.

Step 4 (original G3): clone-G3.next becomes map.get(null) which is null. clone-G3.guarantor becomes map.get(null) which is null.

Step 5: Return map.get(G1), the head of the fully independent copy. Every pointer points into the copy, none into the originals.

sections.s6_takeaway:
Deep-copying a linked list that has both a next pointer and an arbitrary random pointer is tricky because the random pointer can target a node that has not been cloned yet. The cleanest solution is a two-pass HashMap approach. In the first pass I create a clone of every node and store a mapping from each original node to its clone. In the second pass I wire up both pointers on each clone by looking them up in the map, so the clone's next becomes the map value for the original's next, and the clone's random becomes the map value for the original's random. Looking up the map with null conveniently returns null, which handles the end of the list and null random pointers with no special cases. It runs in linear time and linear space.

There is also an elegant interleaving technique that achieves constant extra space by temporarily inserting each clone right after its original, which makes every random target's clone simply its successor, and then unweaving the two lists at the end. I mention it to show I know it, but in practice I usually choose the HashMap version because the interleaving pointer surgery is error-prone and the one real cost, the map, is acceptable.

In my banking project at National Bank of India, we keep a linked chain of loan guarantee records where each record links to the next and also has a guarantor cross-reference to some arbitrary other record. For regulatory archiving we must produce a fully independent frozen copy, and the critical correctness requirement is that every pointer in the copy points into the copy and never back into the live chain, because otherwise a later edit to the live data would silently mutate a supposedly immutable archive.

The subtle point I always call out is that if you use the interleaving method you must carefully restore the original list when you unweave, because you temporarily mutated the caller's data by splicing clones into it, and leaving it corrupted would be a serious side-effect bug in a financial system.
